ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all proposed directors, shareholders, ultimate beneficial owners, and natural-person signatories against the New Zealand Police Financial Intelligence Unit sanctioned and suppressed-persons lists, United Nations Security Council consolidated sanctions, OFAC SDN List, and where commercially practical the EU and UK consolidated sanctions lists. Enhanced due diligence is required for politically exposed persons, their family members, and close associates as defined in section 5 of the AML/CFT Act 2009, including independent verification of source of funds and source of wealth.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Office 'Companies Register' online portal under the Registrar of Companies, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Registered names must be capable of accurate reproduction in the official Companies Register using Latin script. The Companies Office permits English and Maori names and restricts punctuation and symbols. Any non-Latin script must be transliterated into English for the registered legal name.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: A rejected name may be corrected and refiled immediately. If the refusal relates to a conflicting or prohibited name, the applicant may request a Registrar-level manual review within 20 working days, submitting a written rebuttal. If the manual review is unsuccessful, the applicant may pursue judicial review in the High Court of New Zealand under Part 1 of the Companies Act 1993 and the Judicature Amendment Act 1972. Name reservations cannot be extended; the applicant must pay the statutory fee again and file a new reservation.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permitted for an executive search headhunting firm only if the supplier provides a real physical street address in New Zealand where statutory documents may be served and the section 194 Companies Act 1993 registered office obligation is met. A PO Box or digital-only service address is not permitted.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low; estimated probability below 8% per operating year. Unannounced physical inspections are not routine for this non-reporting low-risk sector, but may occur upon a formal complaint, court order, or an AML/CFT supervisory review of an associated reporting entity.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Companies Act 1993 (No. 105 of 1993), particularly sections 10, 12, 16, 21-22, 35-41, 151, 158-161, 201, 211 and Schedule 1; Companies (Incorporation) Regulations 1994; Financial Reporting Act 2013; Income Tax Act 2007; Immigration Advisers Licensing Act 2007.
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: New Zealand Companies Office (NZCO), an independent Crown entity operating within the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), accessible via the New Zealand Companies Register online portal (business.govt.nz/companies).
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Form NCI — Company Incorporation Application (online submission through the RealMe-secured New Zealand Companies Register portal).
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital. A company must allot at least one share to at least one shareholder at incorporation. No escrow account, capital deposit, or solicitor certificate is required; share consideration may be cash, promissory note, or other lawful property under sections 38-41 of the Companies Act 1993.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: FIRST BOARD RESOLUTION OF [●] LIMITED (Adopted in accordance with section 151 of the Companies Act 1993). 1. INCORPORATION AND CONSTITUTION: RESOLVED that the incorporation of the Company under the Companies Act 1993 with the name [●] Limited is ratified and confirmed, and that the Company adopts the default constitution prescribed in Schedule 1 of the Act unless a special constitution has been validly filed with the Registrar. 2. SUBSCRIPTION FOR SHARES: RESOLVED that the proposed allotment of [●] ordinary shares to the subscribers, as recorded in the subscription list, is approved; the Directors are authorised to issue shares, accept consideration and enter the allotment in the share register in accordance with sections 38 to 41 of the Act. 3. REGISTERED OFFICE: RESOLVED that the registered office of the Company be fixed at [physical address in New Zealand] and that the address for service be [address or electronic address], and that the Registrar be notified accordingly. 4. APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS: RESOLVED that [name] be appointed Managing Director, [name] Chairperson and Chief Executive, and [name] Company Secretary, each officer being authorised to act jointly or singly, to open and operate the Company's bank and digital payment accounts including retainer wire and Wise B2B rails. 5. GENERAL POWERS: RESOLVED that the Directors be authorised to procure the common seal, appoint auditors, adopt banking materials, and pay all registration taxes, fees and preliminary expenses.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Company name availability search and reservation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office — name availability check and reservation service on the New Zealand Companies Register portal
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Log in to the New Zealand Companies Register with a RealMe verified account and use the 'Check company names' function to screen the proposed name, including one or two alternative names. Verify that the name is not identical or confusingly similar to an existing registered or reserved name, does not contain offensive or prohibited characters, and does not falsely imply Crown, Government, or statutory endorsement under sections 20-21 of the Companies Act 1993. If a restricted word is used, obtain the written consent of the responsible Ministry and upload the consent letter. Reserve an approved name for up to 20 business days; alternatively, proceed directly to incorporation using the chosen name.
required_dossiers: Proposed company name and up to two alternative names
Name screening report from the NZCO register
Consent letter from the relevant Ministry (only if restricted or sensitive words are used)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar refuses the name for similarity or inappropriateness, the applicant may amend the application and submit a revised name, or apply for an administrative review under section 24 of the Companies Act 1993; if the review is unsuccessful, the applicant may seek judicial review in the High Court of New Zealand.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Preparation of constitutional documents, consents and share subscriptions
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Company legal advisers and New Zealand Companies Office (filings are ultimately lodged through the online register)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Adopt either the default constitution in Schedule 1 of the Companies Act 1993 or a bespoke constitution tailored to the executive search agency's shareholding, director powers and dispute resolution mechanisms. Prepare the share subscription agreement and shareholder register. Obtain signed consent to act as director from each proposed director and a signed consent from the occupier of the registered office address confirming that the physical address is available and open during business hours. All documents must be in English and dated with the proposed incorporation date.
required_dossiers: Constitution (custom or election of statutory default)
Share subscription agreement and allocation schedule
Signed consent to act as director for each proposed director
Signed registered office occupier consent
Photographic identification and proof of address for each director and shareholder (for AML/CFT verification)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If any consent is defective, obtain a corrected signature or a notarised copy from the relevant person; if the constitution conflicts with the Companies Act 1993, revise the offending clauses to comply with section 12 of the Act, otherwise the Registrar will reject the application.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Online incorporation filing and statutory fee payment
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office — online incorporation portal via RealMe and NZBN logon
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete the electronic Company Incorporation Application (Form NCI) on the New Zealand Companies Register. Input the company name, registered office physical address, address for service, constitution election, share structure, and full particulars of shareholders and directors, including at least one director resident in New Zealand or, for a director who is also a director of an Australian company, a physical address in New Zealand. The applicant must declare that the company will comply with the Companies Act 1993. Pay the official incorporation fee of NZD 150.00 by credit card or debit card. On approval, the system automatically issues the Certificate of Incorporation, the NZBN (New Zealand Business Number) and an initial company register summary.
required_dossiers: Completed Form NCI online dataset
Reserved name approval or chosen name
Directors' full legal names, dates of birth, residential addresses and IRD numbers
Shareholders' full legal names, addresses and share allocation
Registered office address and consent record
Address for service details
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the NZCO issues a Notice of Defective Application, the applicant must remedy the identified deficiencies and resubmit within 20 working days; failure to do so may cause the application to be deemed abandoned under section 16(4) of the Companies Act 1993. The applicant may also request a Registrar's review of a refusal, followed by High Court judicial review.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: IR tax registration, NZBN confirmation and GST/PAYE enrolment
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD) via the New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) single sign-on; NZCO issues the NZBN automatically
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Upon incorporation, the NZBN is automatically allocated. Register the company with Inland Revenue using the online 'Register my business' service to obtain an IRD number for income tax. Determine GST liability: registration is compulsory once annual turnover exceeds or is expected to exceed NZD 60,000; registration may be voluntary below that threshold. Register as an employer for PAYE if employees will be engaged and for fringe benefit tax (FBT) if fringe benefits are provided. Select the appropriate tax types and provide the company's bank account details, business activity code (ISIC 7830 / ANZSIC code for executive search) and expected turnover. The IRD issues an IRD number confirmation letter, typically within five business days.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation
NZBN confirmation notice (auto-issued)
Directors' and shareholders' IRD numbers
Declaration of business activity and estimated turnover
Company bank account details (for IRD refunds and tax payments)
GST registration form (IR360) if applicable
Employer (PAYE) registration form if applicable
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If Inland Revenue issues a query or a notice for missing information, respond in writing within the stated deadline (generally 60 days) and provide corrected or supplemented data; a late GST registration can attract penalties under the Tax Administration Act 1994, but the company may apply for voluntary disclosure and remission of penalties by demonstrating reasonable cause.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Registration of registered office and address for service
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office (online company register)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Ensure that the registered office is a physical location in New Zealand that is open to the public and available for receiving documents during ordinary business hours. The address for service may be a physical address, a post office box, or an electronic address such as an email address, and must be maintained on the register at all times. Confirm that the registered office and address for service are recorded in the incorporation application or file an update form if the office is changed. Any change of registered office must be notified to NZCO within 10 working days of the change under section 201 of the Companies Act 1993.
required_dossiers: Lease agreement or title evidence for the registered office location
Signed landlord or occupier consent to use the premises as registered office
Address for service designation form
Notice of change of registered office (if amending after incorporation)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the registered office is found to be invalid or the address for service is defective, immediately file a corrective notice with NZCO and provide an alternative compliant address; persistent failure to maintain a registered office may empower the Registrar to initiate deregistration after six months of non-compliance, which can be remedied by filing annual returns and restoring compliance.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Occupational, fire safety and building compliance for office premises
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Territorial Authority (local city, district or unitary council, e.g., Auckland Council) and Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Verify that the leased office premises are lawfully authorised for commercial office use as a permitted activity under the operative District Plan. Obtain and maintain a current Building Warrant of Fitness (BWOF) for the building, including the annual building inspection certificate and any specified systems compliance schedule under the Building Act 2004. Complete a fire evacuation scheme approval from Fire and Emergency New Zealand if the building has more than 100 occupants or contains high-risk areas. Adopt a compliant Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 management system, appoint a health and safety officer, and conduct electrical, emergency-lighting and means-of-egress inspections. Retain records of building inspections, fire drills and first-aid equipment audits on site.
required_dossiers: Building Warrant of Fitness (BWOF) and annual inspection certificate
Fire evacuation scheme approval (where occupancy thresholds are met)
Health and Safety at Work policy and risk register
Electrical test certificates for office equipment and wiring
Emergency lighting and fire extinguisher maintenance records
Occupational load certificate for office floor areas
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Territorial Authority issues an unsafe building notice or infringement, engage a licensed building practitioner to conduct remedial works and provide a compliance certificate within the notice period; appeal the notice to the District Court under the Building Act 2004 if the notice is disputed; for FENZ refusal of an evacuation scheme, apply for an administrative review by FENZ and then appeal to the District Court.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Industry-specific statutory registration and compliance for executive search and headhunting
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Immigration Advisers Authority (IAA) within the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE); Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) for employer registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Assess whether the company will provide immigration advice as part of its executive search and headhunting services. If the firm employs a person to advise candidates or client companies on immigration matters, that person must hold a New Zealand Licensed Immigration Adviser (LIA) certificate under the Immigration Advisers Licensing Act 2007, or the firm must contract an external licensed adviser. The company must register with the Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) as a statutory employer and pay the applicable employer levy. The company must also comply with the Employment Relations Act 2000, including section 376 which prohibits charging fees to job seekers for finding work, and with the Privacy Act 2020 for the handling of candidate personal data. Maintain a compliance manual evidencing the no-fee-to-candidate model and third-party data processing agreements.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation and NZBN record
Immigration Adviser licence application or engagement agreement with an external licensed immigration adviser
ACC employer registration certificate and levy schedule
Recruitment compliance manual and job-seeker fee prohibition policy
Privacy policy and candidate data protection statements under the Privacy Act 2020
AML/CFT programme documentation (applicable as a reporting entity under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the IAA refuses an immigration adviser licence, the applicant may file for review with the Immigration Advisers Complaints and Disciplinary Tribunal; pending determination, the company may engage an already-licensed adviser to continue lawful cross-border placement services. If ACC queries employer registration, provide payroll projections and employee details to correct the levy assessment; any assessment dispute may be raised with ACC and referred to the District Court if unresolved.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Immigration Advisers Authority (IAA), Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), in conjunction with the Territorial Authority for building and occupancy, Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ), and the Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) for statutory employer registration
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: New Zealand Licensed Immigration Adviser (NZLIA) Certificate — Category 1 or Category 2 under the Immigration Advisers Licensing Act 2007, required where the headhunting service includes cross-border placement or immigration advice; ancillary statutory registrations include the ACC Employer Registration, Building Warrant of Fitness, and the NZCO Certificate of Incorporation, which together constitute the operational licence for an executive search and tech headhunting agency.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) New Zealand and the relevant Territorial Authority under the Resource Management Act 1991
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt — Permitted Activity. No full EIA report, resource consent, or environmental abatement notice is required for an office-based executive search and headhunting agency with no manufacturing, combustion, or trade-waste discharge. A screening note may be recorded under Schedule 4 of the Resource Management Act 1991 if the premises undergo structural alteration or introduce backup diesel generators.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Wastewater must be discharged solely to the municipal reticulated sewerage system and comply with the Water Services Act 2021; trade waste consent is not applicable for office-only operations. Air emissions: ventilation systems must comply with the National Environmental Standards for Air Quality 2004 and AS/NZS 1668.2 indoor air quality standards; no VOC-generating industrial processes are permitted. Noise must not exceed the District Plan permitted activity noise limits (typically 50 dB(A) daytime and 40 dB(A) night-time) at the site boundary. E-waste and fluorescent lamps must be disposed of through a permitted e-waste facility under the Waste Minimisation Act 2008, with disposal records retained for audit.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Building Warrant of Fitness (BWOF) issued by the Territorial Authority under the Building Act 2004, including structural load inspection for the office floor and any dedicated server/record storage area; annual fire safety inspection and approved evacuation scheme from Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) where the occupant load exceeds 100 persons; occupational clearance requires full compliance with the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 and the Health and Safety at Work (General Risk and Workplace Management) Regulations 2016, including electrical safety certificates, first-aid provisions, emergency lighting, fire extinguishers, safe means of egress, and the appointment of a health and safety representative.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD) / Te Tari Taake; online portal: myIR (https://www.ird.govt.nz/myir).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A New Zealand-incorporated limited company is registered with the NZ Companies Office at incorporation and must then apply to the IRD for an IRD number. For a foreign/non-resident company carrying on business in New Zealand, the company applies for an IRD number using the non-resident company application process (form IR742 or via an NZ tax agent) and registers for GST where applicable. The procedure is: (1) incorporate the NZ Ltd or register the overseas company as an NZ branch; (2) obtain a company IRD number from the IRD; (3) register for GST, PAYE, and other applicable tax types through myIR; and (4) appoint a New Zealand agent or nominated principal for tax administration if the company has no physical NZ presence.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation — NZ-resident company taxed on worldwide income at 28% corporate rate; branch of a non-resident company taxed on New Zealand-sourced income at 28%; no US-style pass-through classification as the default for a limited company.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: New Zealand has no 'check-the-box' election for tax classification. Available elections include: (i) voluntary GST registration below the NZD 60,000 threshold; (ii) GST grouping under ss 55-57 of the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985; (iii) look-through company (LTC) status under subpart HA of the Income Tax Act 2007 for closely held NZ-resident companies meeting eligibility criteria; and (iv) consolidated group trading status under the Income Tax Act 2007. Hybrid mismatch adjustments are mandatory under the Taxation (Neutralising Base Erosion and Profit Shifting) Act 2018, not elective.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Value-added-style Goods and Services Tax (GST) under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985, administered by the Inland Revenue Department.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 in any 12-month period for goods and services supplied in New Zealand; a NZD 60,000 threshold also applies to non-resident suppliers of remote/offshore services supplied to New Zealand consumers. Registration may be voluntary below these thresholds (GSTA s 51).
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No statutory real-time fiscal clearance, API clearance, or digital stamping regime is in force. e-Invoicing is voluntary and operates on the PEPPOL standard through the NZ e-Invoicing Service. GST compliance is return-based: registered persons file GST returns through myIR on a monthly, two-monthly, or six-monthly cycle, with no pre-clearance of individual invoices.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Executive search and headhunting services (ISIC 7830) are zero-rated under s 11(1)(m) of the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 when supplied to a non-resident recipient who is outside New Zealand at the time the services are performed and the services are not supplied directly in connection with land or moveable personal property situated in New Zealand. The supplier must hold sufficient documentary evidence, including the supply agreement, tax invoice, and proof of the recipient's non-resident status, to substantiate that the services were performed for the direct benefit of the offshore client. Physical goods exported from New Zealand are zero-rated under s 11(1)(a) if exported within the statutory time frame; for this executive-search service scope, the relevant export rule is the cross-border services provision.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Written engagement or placement agreement with the non-resident client setting out retainer terms, search mandate, and placement fee
Tax invoice or commercial invoice issued in compliance with s 24 of the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985
Evidence of the recipient's non-resident status (overseas VAT/GST registration number, certificate of incorporation, or statutory declaration)
Bank transfer or remittance records showing receipt of retainer and success fees via Retainer_Wire or Wise B2B
Records evidencing offshore execution of the service such as CV submissions, candidate interview logs, and recruiter work performed outside New Zealand
If a physical goods customs flow were involved: NZ Customs export declaration via the Trade Single Window, bill of lading or airway bill, and inward remittance certificate
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: IRD routinely audits export zero-rating claims under s 11(1)(m). If documentation does not establish the non-resident status of the recipient or the offshore consumption of the services, IRD may re-assess the supply at 15% GST, claw back refunded input tax, charge use-of-money interest, and impose shortfall penalties under s 141 of the Tax Administration Act 1994: 20% for lack of reasonable care or an unacceptable tax position, 100% for an abusive tax position, and 150% for evasion. Criminal liability may also arise under ss 143A and 143B of the Tax Administration Act 1994, including fines up to NZD 50,000 for a first evasion offence and responsible director exposure. No statutory time bar applies for fraudulent claims; otherwise IRD may amend assessments within four years of the GST return being filed. In substantive audit practice, IRD applies a 180-day inward-repatriation benchmark to corroborate that foreign-sourced fees were monetised and repatriated to New Zealand.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Te Pūtea Matua), operating in conjunction with the Financial Markets Authority (FMA) and the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) for financial integrity and sanctions administration; however, the Reserve Bank is the sole monetary authority and prudential supervisor for registered banks in New Zealand.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The New Zealand dollar (NZD) is fully convertible for both current and capital account transactions. New Zealand maintains no general exchange-control legislation; dividend repatriation, management fee remittance, shareholder loan repayments, and inbound or outbound equity investments can be executed freely without central bank or exchange-control approval. The only practical requirements are standard anti-money laundering/counter-financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) customer due diligence, tax compliance (e.g. non-resident withholding tax on certain outbound payments), and accurate reporting of offshore balances to Inland Revenue where applicable.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: New Zealand imposes no statutory surrender or mandatory conversion rules for export receipts. Exporters and service providers, including executive-search and headhunting companies, may retain foreign-currency proceeds in offshore accounts or convert them to NZD at any time and at any licensed foreign-exchange dealer. There are no prescribed timelines for repatriation and no minimum conversion percentages. The only relevant obligations arise under general banking AML/CFT reporting thresholds and the requirement that payment instructions accurately state the underlying commercial purpose.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Medium to High viability for cross-border payment execution, subject to important legal constraints. Offshore digital EMI platforms such as Wise Business, Airwallex, and Payoneer are permissible as supplementary payment rails for retainer collections, disbursements, and FX conversion, but they are not licensed New Zealand banks and cannot provide the client with a domestic settlement account protected by the RBNZ banking regulatory framework. To operate meaningfully into New Zealand, the EMI must either be registered on the Financial Service Providers Register (FSPR) and satisfy the AML/CFT Act obligations if carrying on a financial-services business in New Zealand, or the NZ entity must remain the contracting principal and use the EMI solely as an overseas payment gateway. A tier-1 licensed NZ bank account remains the mandatory anchor for capital escrow, statutory record-keeping, and creditor confidence.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: New Zealand AML/CFT law does not categorically require directors to appear physically before a bank. In practice, the major New Zealand banks permit remotely onboarded non-resident directors if reliable digital identity verification (e.g. passport scan with verification software) is combined with certified supporting documents, a registered physical address, and a clear economic-residence explanation. However, for entities with complex ownership structures, non-resident shareholders, or trust/foundation layers, banks typically require at least one director or senior compliance representative to attend an interview, either in a New Zealand branch, at a New Zealand embassy/consulate, or via audio-visual call with a bank compliance officer. This physical-presence mandate arises from internal risk policies rather than explicit statute.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Ultimate beneficial owner (UBO) cannot be identified beyond the immediate New Zealand shareholder.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Companies Office shareholding report; full UBO declaration naming each natural person with beneficial ownership or control above 25%; trust deed or corporate register schedule; certified passports; proof of residential addresses; signed declaration of source of wealth; legal opinion for any discretionary trust.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Initial capital injection to be funded by a non-resident parent or related company with unclear source of funds.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Six to twelve months of parent-company bank statements; executed shareholder loan or subscription agreement; board resolution approving the capital injection; audited financial statements of the parent; invoice or contract explaining any intercompany receivable/payable; personal source-of-funds evidence for individual shareholders.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident director with no New Zealand tax status or with tax residence in a restricted jurisdiction.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified passport and second form of government-issued ID; recent utility bill or bank statement for address verification; tax residency certificate issued by the director's home tax authority; professional reference from a New Zealand lawyer or accountant; explanation of the director's economic nexus to New Zealand and the company's practical management location.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Adverse media, sanctions-list, or politically exposed person (PEP) flags on any director, shareholder, or counterparty.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Full sanctions screening results conducted through a licensed screening provider; adverse-media search report with explanations for any matches; independent compliance review; PEP declaration form; remediation evidence such as resignation of affected director or divestment of affected shareholder; legal opinion on the relevance of any past enforcement action.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Business model mismatch or lack of verifiable revenue for an executive-search / headhunting operation.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Signed retainer agreements with client companies; standard fee schedule and placement invoices; proof of the statutory licence/registration where required; GST registration certificate; employer identification records; management accounts or projected cash-flow statements; evidence of business premises or virtual-office arrangement; professional indemnity insurance policy.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound shareholder loans and equity injections should be routed by SWIFT MT103 or SWIFT MT202 from the foreign parent/shareholder to the New Zealand company's licensed bank account. The payment reference field must clearly state the economic purpose, preferably as 'Share Capital Contribution', 'Paid-Up Equity', or 'Director/Owner Loan'. No statutory New Zealand purpose-code regime exists; however, receiving banks map remittance information to internal transaction categories, and the company must be ready to provide the executed subscription agreement, board resolution, updated share register, and an AML/CFT source-of-funds explanation if requested. Cross-currency inbound wires are automatically converted by the receiving bank or a corresponding bank at the onshore NZD interbank rate unless an alternative settlement currency has been specifically agreed. No Reserve Bank approval or exchange-control permit is required.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Operational trade disbursements and retainer payments to overseas executive-search partners should be executed via SWIFT MT103 through the New Zealand bank's correspondent network. For high-value recruitment settlement between corporates, a Commercial Letter of Credit (UCP600) can be issued by the NZ company's bank in favour of an overseas beneficiary after presentation of a signed placement invoice, employment agreement, and candidate start/deal-sheet evidence. NZD-denominated domestic legs of any such transaction settle over the Exchange Settlement Account System (ESAS), the country's high-value payment system, with the cross-border leg completed through the SWIFT network. Supporting documents for outbound disbursements include the underlying retainer contract, invoice, candidate acceptance evidence, and a valid GST tax invoice. Non-resident withholding tax and approved issuer levy treatment must be considered if the payment contains interest, fees, or similar periodic amounts.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: FX Vanilla Option (call/put on NZD crosses)

Non-Deliverable Forward (NDF) for illiquid or restricted emerging-market currency pairs where onshore deliverability is unavailable; NZD NDFs are typically offered offshore given the mature onshore deliverable market

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return (corporate declaration confirming directors, shareholders, shareholdings, registered office, address for service, and NZBN details)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office (Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due within 20 working days after the company's balance date; standard statutory balance date is 31 March, making the usual due date late April
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Automatic NZ$150 late-filing penalty; each director liable to a court-imposed fine up to NZ$10,000; two consecutive years of non-filing triggers administrative strike-off under ss.336–343 of the Companies Act 1993, with all company property vesting in the Crown upon removal.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Financial statements for the accounting period (audited where mandatory), filed with the Annual Return or otherwise made available to shareholders under the small-company exemption
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registrar of Companies (via the Companies Office); presented to shareholders and to the Financial Markets Authority where the company is an FMC reporting entity
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within the same Annual Return filing period (20 working days after balance date) when filing is required; otherwise financial statements must be prepared and presented to shareholders within 6 months of balance date
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Directors contravene the Financial Reporting Act 2013 and may be fined up to NZ$10,000; continued non-compliance may be referred to the FMA or used by the Registrar to support company removal proceedings.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: Mandatory independent audit applies to (1) FMC reporting entities under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013; (2) 'large' companies under s.45 of the Financial Reporting Act 2013, i.e. total assets exceeding NZ$30 million or total revenue exceeding NZ$50 million in each of the two preceding accounting periods; and (3) any company whose shareholders holding at least 5% of voting rights validly require an audit under s.199 of the Companies Act 1993. Small (total assets and revenue not exceeding NZ$2.25 million) and medium companies remain generally audit-exempt unless one of these triggers is satisfied.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: External Reporting Board (XRB) for-profit Accounting Standards Framework: Tier 1 applies NZ IFRS (full IFRS equivalence); Tier 2 applies NZ IFRS with Reduced Disclosure Regime; Tier 3 small entities apply the simplified NZ IFRS for SMEs. Preparation and filing obligations are governed by the Financial Reporting Act 2013 and the Companies Act 1993.

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 28% (resident companies and non-resident companies carrying on business through a New Zealand branch, under Income Tax Act 2007, Schedule 1, Part A)
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No general statutory tax holidays. Available incentives include: 15% R&D tax credit on eligible R&D expenditure; R&D loss tax credit for early-stage companies; immediate expensing of low-value assets up to NZ$5,000; depreciation loading for certain assets; imputation credit system to prevent economic double taxation of distributed profits.
corporate_income_tax_regime.tax_loss_carryforward_limit_years: Indefinite (subject to a 49% minimum shareholder continuity requirement; if continuity is breached, the 'same or similar business' test may permit continued carry-forward under limited conditions)

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: IR4 – Company Income Tax Return; filed electronically through the Inland Revenue myIR secure online portal (www.ird.govt.nz) or by paper if IRD-approved.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual (income year of 12 months; a substituted accounting balance date may be approved by the IRD)
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Standard balance date (31 March): online IR4 filing due by 7 July immediately following the end of the income year; paper filing due by 7 June. For a substituted balance date, the filing date is adjusted correspondingly; tax agents with an Extension of Time arrangement may file as late as 31 March of the following year.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: IR4 – Company Details Section (IRD number, legal name, balance date)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Identify the entity as a New Zealand resident company or non-resident company branch; record the registered balance date and IRD number.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use the New Zealand IRD number assigned to the branch or company. For a non-resident company, ensure the full legal name of the foreign parent and any New Zealand branch address are disclosed.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: IR4 – Income Section (Gross income / revenue lines)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Include gross income from executive search and headhunting services: retainer fees, success fees, contracted placement commissions, and any activities performed in New Zealand.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident companies must report only New Zealand-source income. Clearly attribute fees to services performed in New Zealand or services performed offshore for NZ clients, following the source rules in sections YD 4 and YD 4B.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Claim deductions for salaries and subcontractor search consultants, advertising, job-board database fees, travel, telecommunications, rent, and any expenses directly incurred in producing assessable income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident branches may deduct only expenses actually incurred in deriving New Zealand-source income. Apportion shared global headhunting database and management costs on a just and reasonable basis; related-party expenses are subject to transfer pricing and thin capitalisation rules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: IR4 – Taxable Income / Loss Calculation and Loss Carry-forward
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Compute net taxable profit or loss after applying allowable deductions, depreciation, and any brought-forward tax losses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident companies may carry forward losses derived from their New Zealand branch only if they satisfy continuity requirements and file all relevant schedules. Losses of a foreign entity cannot be used against New Zealand income unless the entity is a fully resident NZ company.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: IR4 – Tax Reconciliation and Credits Section (Provisional tax, RWT, imputation credits, tax credits)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Reconcile income tax payable with provisional tax already paid, resident withholding tax on interest/dividends, imputation credits attached to dividends, and any R&D tax credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-residents cannot generally claim imputation credits unless they are NZ resident or use a portfolio investment entity exemption; include any non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) paid at source on New Zealand interest or dividends. Claim treaty relief only where a valid certificate of residence is held.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty (LFP) of NZ$250 for each month or part-month the IR4 remains unfiled, subject to a maximum cap under the Tax Administration Act 1994. In addition, late payment penalties apply on any unpaid residual income tax: an initial late payment penalty of 1% of the unpaid tax; a further late payment penalty of 1% for each subsequent month or part-month the tax remains outstanding; and use-of-money interest (UOMI) accrues daily on underpaid tax and shortfall tax at IRD-prescribed rates.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: Non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) on dividends is 30% on gross dividends; where the dividend is fully imputed and paid to a non-resident, the NRWT rate is 15%. Under many double tax agreements (DTAs), a full or reduced rate (often 15% or 0% for substantial corporate shareholdings above 10%) may be available. Dividends paid to NZ-resident companies are not subject to NRWT but may attract resident withholding tax (RWT) at 28% for companies or 33% for individuals if imputation credits are insufficient.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke DTA relief, the non-resident recipient must obtain from its country of tax residence an official Certificate of Residence (TRC) or equivalent tax authority document containing the recipient’s name and tax identification number. The New Zealand payer must retain a copy of the TRC before applying the reduced rate. If the DTA rate has not been applied at source, the non-resident may file a claim with Inland Revenue for a refund of excess NRWT within the statutory limitation period (generally four years from the end of the tax year in which the payment was made). For interest flows, an Approved Issuer Levy (AIL) of 2% may be elected in place of NRWT if the NZ payee is an approved issuer and the interest is paid on registered money lending instruments.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Domestic NRWT is 15% on cross-border interest and 15% on royalties paid to non-residents. Under many NZ DTAs, interest is typically reduced to 10% and royalties to 10% or 5%; where a payment is made to a resident of a treaty country, the domestic rate is overridden by the treaty rate, subject to beneficial ownership and TRC requirements. Inbound and outbound related-party interest and royalty payments must be priced on an arm's length basis, and the amounts paid may be recharacterised if they are not at arm's length.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: New Zealand does not maintain a universally codified master/local file system with a fixed pecuniary threshold. Under the Taxation (Neutralising Base Erosion and Profit Shifting) Act 2018 and IRD practice, contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation is expected where the aggregate value of cross-border related-party transactions exceeds NZ$10 million in an income year; in assessing penalties, the IRD will consider whether the taxpayer has kept sufficient documentation to support the arm's length outcome. Country-by-Country (CbC) reporting applies to multinational groups with consolidated group revenue of at least EUR 750 million (approximately NZ$1.3 billion).
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand does not apply Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) as used in similar offshore jurisdictions. However, the OECD substance concept is embedded in the general anti-avoidance rule (GAAR) under section BG 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007: arrangements lacking genuine commercial substance that are structured primarily to defeat tax are void against the Commissioner. Economic substance also determines treaty residence for dual-resident companies under Article 4 of DTAs (place of effective management) and can trigger the re-assessment of a New Zealand company as resident or non-resident where board control, management functions, and physical presence are displaced.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Deliberately understating executive-search fee income; inflating non-deductible entertainment or sham placement expenses; diverting NZ-source fees to a related offshore tax haven company; destroying records or making false declarations in the IR4; structuring services so that fees are booked offshore while all negotiation and delivery occurs in New Zealand.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Shortfall penalties under the Tax Administration Act 1994: 100% of the tax shortfall for an abusive tax position; 150% for evasion or similar conduct. Criminal prosecution may result in fines up to NZ$50,000 and imprisonment for up to 5 years. Interest and late payment penalties are also assessed from the original due date.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly participate in tax evasion or false filing can be prosecuted in their personal capacity and cannot hide behind the corporate veil. The court may impose civil restitution, award compensation orders, and issue asset-restraint or forfeiture orders. Directors charged with serious tax offences may face travel restrictions as a bail condition and imprisonment upon conviction.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company / Lack of Economic Substance
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating a New Zealand limited company with nominee directors, no office, no employees, and no commercial records, used solely as an invoicing vehicle for overseas headhunting activities; engaging in 'phoenix' liquidation to escape tax liabilities; misrepresenting the company as non-resident to avoid NZ taxation while essential management and control sit in New Zealand.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The Commissioner may invoke the GAAR (section BG 1) to disregard the arrangement and assess the true profit-maker. The company may be treated as a New Zealand tax resident if its centre of effective management is in NZ, with resulting worldwide income taxation. Phoenix-company penalties, director disqualification, and liquidation powers under the Companies Act 1993 also apply; financial penalties may reach NZ$100,000 plus reinstated tax and penalties.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors can be personally liable for insolvent trading under sections 131 and 135 of the Companies Act 1993, and for unpaid PAYE/GST-related liabilities if the company is wound up and has failed to meet statutory obligations. The corporate veil is pierced where the company is a mere façade; directors may be ordered to pay civil restitution from personal assets, disqualified from managing companies for up to 5 years, and restricted from leaving New Zealand pending insolvency or criminal investigations.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Setting non-arm's length success fees, management fees, or intercompany administrative mark-ups with a related offshore entity; loading the New Zealand headhunting company with excessive shareholder debt and paying above-market interest; allocating global search-database costs to the NZ entity without evidence of benefit; choosing a TP method that produces a systematically low NZ margin.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: IRD will adjust the taxable income to an arm's length outcome under sections GC 13–GC 16 of the Income Tax Act 2007, disallow excess interest deductions under thin capitalisation rules, and impose shortfall penalties. If the taxpayer has not taken reasonable care, a 20% penalty applies; for unacceptable tax positions, a 20%–50% penalty may apply; if the dominant purpose is tax avoidance, the penalty can be 100%–150%.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who design and approve sham transfer-pricing arrangements can be made personally liable for shortfall penalties if they are found to be the directing mind behind the avoidance. In liquidation, the Commissioner may claim against directors for breach of duty of care, and directors may face personal civil awards for losses caused by reckless trading and misrepresentation. Travel bans and imprisonment can follow if the conduct is also prosecuted as tax evasion.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Profit Repatriation / Dividend Stripping and Unpaid NRWT
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Paying dividends, interest, or royalties to a foreign parent or related party without deducting NRWT; disguising an accumulation of profits as a capital return or loan on-charge; selling New Zealand shares to a foreign affiliate to strip accumulated profits as a capital gain instead of a dividend; failing to attach imputation credits falsely to reduce NRWT.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: IRD will recharacterise the distribution as a dividend or interest under the anti-avoidance provisions and assess NRWT at the applicable domestic or treaty rate (up to 30% on dividends; 15% on interest/royalties), plus UOMI, late payment penalties, and shortfall penalties. Directors of trustees or intermediaries involved in NRWT evasion may be jointly assessed as agents under the Tax Administration Act 1994.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors can be personally liable for unremitted NRWT where the company has acted as a withholding agent or where the arrangement is a sham. They face civil recovery of the evaded tax, director disqualification, asset-freezing orders, and, in cases of deliberate evasion, detention or travel restriction pending trial and imprisonment upon conviction. The corporate veil is pierced where distributions are made to defeat a creditor, including the Crown.
